Indian cricket drives APAC automotive sports sponsorship to $359.5 million
article_text:
Indian cricket accounted for more than a third of Asia-Pacific automotive sports sponsorship spending in 2025, with brands investing US$122.9 million in partnerships linked to the sport, according to a new report by GlobalData.

The report puts total automotive sports sponsorship spending across the region at US$359.5 million in 2025, a 64.7 per cent increase since 2020. Cricket contributed more than two-thirds of the market’s growth over the five-year period, reflecting the commercial appeal of major competitions and their large audiences.

The Indian Premier League (IPL) and the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) have been key attractions for automotive brands seeking exposure in the Indian market.

GlobalData’s Sponsorship Sector Report – Automotive – APAC 2026 found that 46.3 per cent of the region’s sponsorship deal value in 2025 came from 11 agreements worth at least US$5 million each. The number of active automotive brands involved in sponsorships across Asia-Pacific also rose from 117 in 2020 to 274 in 2025.

The report also points to a concentration of spending among a relatively small number of major partnerships. Eleven deals valued at US$5 million or more accounted for 46.3 per cent of the total deal value in 2025.

GlobalData sport analyst Olivia Snooks said cricket’s reach in India was attracting automotive companies looking to connect with large audiences.

“India cricket accounted for three of the top 10 largest automotive deals across the region in 2025, including Tata Motors’ IPL title sponsorship deal, which is the largest across APAC,” she said.

The report identified 69 brands entering APAC automotive sports sponsorship for the first time in 2025, across 71 deals. Japanese brands accounted for 36 of those deals, while 10 involved Chinese brands. Many were smaller arrangements involving major team sports, including the IPL, Australia’s National Rugby League (NRL) and Australian Football League (AFL). Others involved motorsport and events such as the Asian Le Mans Series and the Olympic movement.

However, new entrants were outnumbered in financial terms by brands leaving the market. GlobalData said 62 brands with active partnerships in 2024 exited in 2025, taking more than twice the deal value brought in by new sponsors. The largest departure was Roewe’s reported US$8 million exit, which was offset by the entry of its parent company, SAIC Motor.

The report also found different approaches among the largest automotive sponsors. Tata Motors committed US$64.3 million across three high-value deals, while Toyota spent US$33.4 million across 11 partnerships.

Tata Motors and Apollo Tyres focused on fewer, larger sponsorship agreements, particularly in cricket. Toyota and tyre manufacturer BKT pursued a broader portfolio of partnerships across different sports and markets.

Over the five years to 2025, automotive sponsorship spending in APAC grew at an average annual rate of 10.5 per cent, according to GlobalData. Apollo Tyres recorded growth of 67.4 per cent, Tata Motors 52.6 per cent and Nissan 36.4 per cent. Hyundai, Hero MotoCorp and Yamaha reduced their spending over the same period.

Snooks said the figures showed how automotive brands were taking different approaches, with some increasing investment in major sporting properties while others scaled back or spread their spending across a larger number of partnerships.

The findings point to cricket’s growing commercial pull in India, particularly for brands seeking national exposure through major competitions. However, the wider APAC market remains varied, with sponsorship strategies shaped by local audiences, sporting interests and the value of individual deals.

All financial figures are in US dollars, as reported by GlobalData. The figures reflect the research firm’s sponsorship deal estimates and should not be read as audited expenditure by the brands.

title: Alexander Zverev: German 'annoyed' by reaction to him becoming world number one
article_text:
Alexander Zverev says he has been "annoyed" by the reaction to him becoming world number one.

The German, 29, claims he is the only tennis player who "has to explain why it's OK" for him to be top of the rankings.

Zverev lost to Italy's Lorenzo Musetti at the Paris Masters on Wednesday - his first match since becoming the ATP Tour's number one for the first time.

He has won his first two Grand Slams titles in 2026, but his success has come in a year in which Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner have struggled with injuries.

"I don't think anybody had to explain themselves as much as I had to do in the last couple of days, which for me, is annoying, to be honest," Zverev said.

Zverev has a 62-8 win-loss record against opponents ranked 11 and below in the world this year - but he has only won three of 12 matches against top-10 players.

Before this year's French Open, Sinner and Alcaraz had shared the past nine Grand Slam titles, with Sinner beating Zverev in last year's Australian Open final.

Zverev has lost in each of his 10 most recent meetings with Sinner, who has not played since Wimbledon after injuring his knee and has subsequently dropped to number two in the rankings.

He has also lost four of his past five matches against Alcaraz, who missed large parts of the season with a wrist injury.

"I was a bit annoyed, to be honest, because achieving the world number one status is something that every player dreams of," said Zverev, who won this year's French Open and US Open titles and lost to Sinner in the final of Wimbledon.

"But then I feel like I'm the only world number in tennis history that has to explain why it's OK for me to be world number one, which I find quite difficult, because I think I deserve to be where I am, even though I lost today."

Zverev did not specify which issues had been annoying him after going to the top of the rankings.

His ascent has led to previous accusations of physical abuse by two of his former partners being highlighted again.

Zverev has always firmly maintained his innocence and has insisted the allegations are baseless.

He was presented with the world number one trophy in Paris on Monday but, after receiving a bye through the first round, was beaten 7-6 (7-5) 6-2 by Musetti.

Looking at his performance on Wednesday, Zverev said: "To simplify it, he played really good and I played really bad.

"I think this was not a very good match from me, I think it might be one of the worst in the last couple of months."

title: Pegula calls Andreeva 'diva' after practice session
article_text:
The Women's Tennis Association says it takes "full responsibility" for not telling players there were microphones on practice courts after private comments Jessica Pegula made to her coach about fellow player Mirra Andreeva were live-streamed.

The session at Indian Wells, California, was streamed by the WTA before its Tour Finals start on Sunday.

In a private conversation with her coach Mark Knowles, world number five Pegula described Andreeva as "a diva".

The American could also be heard saying the French Open champion "needs to be humbled" and her coach Conchita Martinez encourages her behaviour.

Pegula's agent, Chris McCormack, said she had been "completely unaware" the conversation could be heard by courtside microphones, "let alone live-streamed to the public".

"Naturally it's been an unfortunate situation for everyone involved," McCormack told BBC Sport.

"Jess has since been in direct contact with those involved, which she felt was important to do personally rather than through the media."

YouTube streams of Wednesday's practice sessions at Indian Wells have since been removed by the WTA, but the footage had already been shared on social media.

It is understood the microphones were only intended to capture the sounds of rallies and not any conversations on court, and there will be no audio on future videos.

"The WTA takes full responsibility for failing to inform our players and their teams that microphones, in place to give fans a livestream of the players' practice, were active on the courts at the WTA Finals," a statement read.

"We sincerely apologise for failing to meet our responsibility to ensure players and coaches were properly informed."

Pegula, who is a member of the WTA players' council, also praised Andreeva, saying the world number three is "wonderful" and "smart".

The season-ending WTA Finals, being held at Indian Wells for the first time, run until 15 November.

Pegula's representative and the WTA have been approached for comment.

In a separate incident, world number one Elena Rybakina appeared to have an angry exchange with her coach before a practice session with Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova.

Some of the audio is unclear, but Pegula can be heard describing how Andreeva and Martinez complained throughout the session, even though Andreeva won every game.

Pegula: "Conchita's always been very nice to me, but I've lost a little respect for her because I'm like, this girl - I think she's a nice girl - she's just a diva. She needs to be humbled. She needs to be [inaudible] putting her in her place; [inaudible] stand up to her."

Spaniard Martinez - the 1994 Wimbledon champion - began working with Andreeva in April 2024. Andreeva reached the Wimbledon quarter-finals last year and claimed her first Grand Slam title at Roland Garros in June.

Pegula: "Conchita pokes her and eggs on her behaviour."

Knowles: "She needs somebody to put her in her place. Once she gets that, I think she'll be really good. I mean, she's already really good. Look how she moves."

Pegula: "She moves like a cat. She's wonderful. She's got the perfect serve. She's smart. She anticipates well."

Pegula, who has not won a Grand Slam, then compared Andreeva to world number four Coco Gauff. The American was also 19 when she won her first Grand Slam. Now 22, she has won two majors.

Pegula: "It's so funny how you see her and then you see Coco's mentality. If she had Coco's mentality, she'd be better than her."

Pegula: "The serve, everything, all-around, and she moves just as good. But like mentally, she's..."

Pegula and Andreeva are in different groups at the WTA Finals but could meet in the semi-finals or final.

Pegula's group opponents are Gauff, Rybakina and Noskova, and the latter pair's practice session at Indian Wells was also live-streamed.

Australian and US Open champion Rybakina appears to remonstrate with coach Stefano Vukov as they walk to the net, saying: "Stay here. I'm talking to you. Can you stand here?"

They shared a few more words, which are inaudible, before going to the other side of the court together to greet Noskova and her team.

Vukov was suspended by the WTA in February 2025 following an independent investigation into his behaviour towards Kazakhstan's Rybakina. He returned to her team that August.

Pegula was among the players to complain about additional behind-the-scenes cameras at the Australian Open in January.

The semi-finalist described the filming as an "invasion of privacy" that needs to be "cut back".

"You just feel like you're under a microscope constantly," she said.

title: “Everyone is probably cooked”: Shelton feels 100 per cent for the first time since the US Open
article_text:
Ben Shelton said this is the first week since the US Open in which he has felt 100 per cent ready to compete, after reaching the Rolex Paris Masters quarter-finals as several top players fell early.

Ben Shelton believes most players are running on empty at the end of the season, but he says he is not one of them any more. After coming from a set down to beat Arthur Rinderknech 3-6, 6-4, 7-6 (5) in the last 16 of the Rolex Paris Masters on Thursday, the World No. 4 said this was the first week since the US Open that he had felt ready to compete at 100 per cent.

Asked whether players were exhausted at this time of the season, with several top-10 players already out in Paris, Shelton told reporters, including Tennis Majors: “Yeah, I think everyone is probably cooked. For me, after the US Open I was really cooked, going to Davis Cup and then China for Shanghai. This is kind of the first week since the US Open that I’ve really felt 100 per cent ready to compete, and I’m super excited to be here.”

Shelton reached his first Grand Slam final at the US Open, where he lost to Alexander Zverev 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2. In his next two tournaments, he lost in his second match in Shanghai, to Frenchman Arthur Gea, and in Basel last week, to Swiss Jerome Kym in a final-set tie-break.

In Paris, he has beaten Cameron Norrie 6-3, 6-4 and Rinderknech, his 43rd win of 2026, a personal best for a season. He faces fellow American Tommy Paul in the quarter-finals on Friday.

Shelton’s words come after a day of upsets on Wednesday, when World No. 1 Alexander Zverev, Daniil Medvedev, Alex de Minaur and Frances Tiafoe all lost their opening matches, and Novak Djokovic was knocked out by qualifier Rinky Hijikata. Medvedev described the Paris tournament as a puzzle after his defeat to Ignacio Buse.

For the first time since the tournament’s inaugural edition, 40 years ago, no former Paris semi-finalist made it to the last 16.

“Obviously we have a really long schedule, and some guys are already looking forward to their vacation,” Shelton said. “For me, […] it’s a blessing and a huge motivation.”

Shelton is already qualified for the Nitto ATP Finals in Turin (November 15-22), the last event of the season. He will share that stage with a close friend: Arthur Fils, who qualified for the ATP Finals for the first time on Wednesday.

“I think he’s had an outstanding season, especially with the tournaments where he’s been injured and missed, but also the tournaments where people don’t know he was injured and playing through injury,” Shelton said. “I’m really happy for him, just super excited for him to get his first chance in Turin. I think he’s playing at such a high level, he’s improving every year, and we’re really close friends. So I’m going to enjoy getting to share that with him this year, and hopefully some other Americans as well.”

title: PV Sindhu 'happy to be back' in top 6 rankings: Ace shuttler won 2 titles in 2026; speaks on husband's supp...
article_text:
PV Sindhu has been one of Indian badminton's biggest flag-bearers for well over a decade now. 2026 has been a year of mixed returns for Sindhu. The two-time Olympic medallist has won two titles this year so far.

In July, Sindhu won the Japan Open title, becoming the first Indian to win the tournament. Most recently, she captured the Hylo Open crown in Germany. Having had a year of highs and lows, Sindhu looks back at the year, which has given her confidence and passion to keep pushing herself.

Bhaskar English was part of an interaction with Sindhu, where she spoke about her performance this year, the support she has received from her husband and the future of Indian badminton.

The Hylo Open victory in Germany made her the first Indian woman to win the title. The victory also propelled her back into the top 6 in the BWF World Rankings. This is her highest ranking since October 2022, when she was number five. "I am happy to be back inside the top six again," she said, while responding to a query by Bhaskar English.

Expressing gratitude to her team and family for their unwavering support, the 31-year-old added, "I have been working on myself, my game and the support I received from my team has been very, very important in making sure that the body is 100%. I am very grateful that I have an amazing team. Of course, my family's support and my in-laws' support are always there."

A year of highs and lows like 2026 has made Sindhu realise that there's still room for improvement. "What I would take from this year is the confidence and the passion that I can still keep pushing myself. There's a lot more room for improvement. I am getting there. I am happy, in a good space mentally and physically," she said.

Having achieved the No. 6 ranking, is the No. 1 rank on her mind? A look at her BWF page shows her sporting ambition: 'To become world No. 1'. However, she is aware that it would come through consistent performances. The ace shuttler now has her sights firmly set on the BWF World Tour Finals 2026, which is slated to take place in Hangzhou, China, from 9 to 13 December. "I will be focusing on that," she said. This is the first time since 2021 that Sindhu has made it to the competition.

Badminton is an extremely physically demanding sport, and at 31, Sindhu is aware that she is not getting any younger. Although Sindhu's love and passion for the sport remains strong as ever, she understands the importance of taking care of her body.

After winning the Hylo Open, Sindhu opted to pull out of the Korea Open and Japan Masters, choosing rest and recovery after playing back-to-back competitions. "It was important for me to take care of my body, come back and then again get fit for the next tournaments," she said.

"Initially, the plan was, I'll be playing other tournaments as well. But I think it was important for me to make the decision that I would not be playing. Because it was important that I need to also take care of my body and get back stronger on court again. I'm not young anymore. But also, 31 is new 21. I need to take care of my body, don't I?" added Sindhu.

Days ago, Sindhu posted an Instagram story, sharing a photo of her husband, Venkata Datta Sai, where she wrote that she married 'her biggest cheerleader'. Sindhu married Sai in 2024 in a dreamy ceremony in Udaipur.

The ace shuttler lavished praise on her partner for his support in her career. "I am grateful. I am lucky to have him. He also played a major role. He got all this team together and made things work. And I think I'm lucky in a way my parents are very supportive," she said. The 31-year-old further explained how her husband understands sports and the highs and lows that an athlete faces. His constant feedback is also something that helps Sindhu improve.

"He travels for some of the tournaments. He also understands sports. I'm grateful because as a partner, you need someone who understands sports to know what you're going through in those moments where you're really at your lowest at times. And, you know, sometimes he tells me if I'm making any mistakes. He just gives his opinions. It's always nice to know some of the inputs from outside when people observe and see your match a lot more times," she said.

While Sindhu has remained the undisputed flag-bearer of Indian badminton for quite a few years now, the country has been blessed with a newer crop of players who have shown that the nation's future in badminton is in safe hands.

At the Hylo Open, Sindhu defeated 19-year-old Anmol Kharb in the semifinals on her way to the title. Kharb had defeated another promising 19-year-old, Unnati Hooda, in the quarters. "I am happy to see a lot of youngsters doing well. Ashmita (Chaliha) had done really well, and Anmol had been doing really well," Sindhu said.

“Of course, Unnati and Tanvi (Sharma). So, we are seeing a lot of youngsters, and I am really happy that there are 4-5 girls who are coming up and are doing really well and representing the country. What else do we need?” she said.

title: Race To Dubai Leader Eugenio Chacarra Forced Into Untimely Driver Change
article_text:
Race To Dubai leader Eugenio Chacarra struggled to find a fairway during the first round at the Abu Dhabi Championship as he was forced to play with a replacement driver.

It wasn't the ideal start for the biggest two weeks of Chacarra's career, as he looks to hold off Patrick Reed and Rory McIlroy and become just the third Spaniard to win the Harry Vardon Trophy.

The 26-year-old cracked his regular driver during the Pro-Am in Abu Dhabi and the replacement club wasn't behaving as he missed every fairway on the front nine.

Despite the radar being dodgy off the tee, Chacarra still managed to shoot a two-under 70 at Yas Links with no real damage done to his Race To Dubai chances as McIlroy was was given a two-shot penalty to also finish with a 70, while Reed had a nightmare finish in his 74.

"I got a bit unlucky that my driver cracked yesterday in the Pro-Am on the 6th hole, and I can't really find a fairway," Chacarra told Sky Sports' Tim Barter during an on-course interview at Yas Links.

"It's tough out here if you're from the rough. The greens are pretty firm if you attack from the rough."

Playing alongside McIlroy and Reed as the three Race To Dubai challengers went head-to-head on Thursday, Chacarra turned things around on the back nine with four of his six birdies coming home.

McIlroy had thought he'd stolen a march on Chacarra when he signed for a 68, but that was later turned into a 70 when his double-bogey six on the 12th became a quadruple-bogey eight thanks to his two-shot penalty.

After a failed chip rolled back down a slope into a divot, close-up TV replays showed McIlroy's wedge had pressed some grass down behind his ball when he addressed it - which was adjudged to have improved his lie.

McIlroy accepted his penalty while insisting it was not a deliberate act, but regardless it hurt his chances of closing the gap on Chacarra as he chases a fifth victory in a row and record-equalling eighth European No.1 finish.

After plotting his way around Yas Links, McIlroy only stepped on the gas after his problems at the 12th, as he reeled off a hat-trick of birdies on 14, 15 and 16 to ensure he finished above Chacarra. Or so he thought.

By contrast, Reed could only manage one birdie in his largely uneventful round which saw him card 10 straight pars before a birdie at 11, bogey at 14 and then the most annoying finish possible with a double on the last.

Francesco Laporta leads the way after the first round following a brilliant 62 while Jon Rahm shot 65 on his return to action - he's T2 alongside Englishman Sam Bairstow who was the last man into the field following a string of withdrawals.

Bairstow finished 81st on the Race To Dubai with only the top 70 to qualify for Abu Dhabi, but with 11 players dropping out he found out on the plane over to the UAE that he'd bagged a place in the field - and he's making the most of it.

Paul Higham is a sports journalist with over 20 years of experience in covering most major sporting events for both Sky Sports and BBC Sport. He is currently freelance and covers the golf majors on the BBC Sport website. Highlights over the years include covering that epic Monday finish in the Ryder Cup at Celtic Manor and watching Rory McIlroy produce one of the most dominant Major wins at the 2011 US Open at Congressional. He also writes betting previews and still feels strangely proud of backing Danny Willett when he won the Masters in 2016 - Willett also praised his putting stroke during a media event before the Open at Hoylake. Favourite interviews he's conducted have been with McIlroy, Paul McGinley, Thomas Bjorn, Rickie Fowler and the enigma that is Victor Dubuisson. A big fan of watching any golf from any tour, sadly he spends more time writing about golf than playing these days with two young children, and as a big fair weather golfer claims playing in shorts is worth at least five shots. Being from Liverpool he loves the likes of Hoylake, Birkdale and the stretch of tracks along England's Golf Coast, but would say his favourite courses played are Kingsbarns and Portrush.

The UK-based Icons Series has signed a two-year partnership with Heineken Beverages for the Icons Cup South Africa, a team match-play golf event at The Links at Fancourt in George from 11th to 13th December. Former England footballer John Terry and former England cricketer Jimmy Anderson are among the players.

Three Heineken Beverages brands are involved. Windhoek Beer is the event’s beer partner, Savanna Cider its cider partner and Amarula Liqueur its cream liqueur partner. Windhoek will run the 19th Hole, a new hospitality area where players and spectators gather after each day’s play. Savanna and Amarula will host fan zones and viewing areas around the course.

The deal also covers activity before the event. Heineken Beverages will also support the partnership with paid media, broadcast integrations and in-store activations.

The Icons Series was founded by Thomas Brookes, a former agent at International Sports Management, and stages match-play golf events featuring athletes from other sports. It has strong UK ties: it has held events including ICONS of Rugby at The Buckinghamshire Golf Club, and its Icons of Football event at Reignwood Park in Bangkok, featuring a Team England side, was shown on Sky Sports in 2025 and 2026.

Thomas Brookes, CEO and Founder of the Icons Series, said, “The way we have worked together over the past few months has shaped this into the exciting collaboration it has become. Kavir Gangiah, Head of Consumer Experience and Sponsorships at Heineken Beverages, said, “The Icons Cup brings together world-class game-changers in an authentic environment, making it the perfect fit for Heineken Beverages and our brand portfolio.”

Heineken were also a partner of the 2026 SIAs.

title: Nelly Korda arrives on Hall of Fame’s doorstep — without playing
article_text:
Field lists don’t usually make history, but that’s exactly what happened at 5 p.m. Tuesday when the participants in the LPGA’s penultimate event of 2026, the Annika, were finalized. Absent from the field were Jeeno Thitikul and Miyu Yamashita, the second- and fourth-ranked players in the women’s game, respectively, meaning, after outstanding seasons, they had mathematically eliminated themselves from the LPGA’s Rolex Player of the Year race — and determined a winner.

That would be world No. 2 Nelly Korda, in the wake of her four-win (so far) 2026 and still with three events remaining on the schedule. This is Korda’s second time winning the prize; when she won her first POY, in 2024, she also locked up the title with three events remaining on the schedule.

This year’s accolade, though, comes with an added wrinkle, because it pushed Korda to within sniffing distance of the LPGA Hall of Fame. POY winners don’t just win a trophy and a year-end gala shoutout — they also get a point toward their Hall of Fame eligibility. In Korda’s case, that point increases her career point haul to 26, which is just one shy of the HOF entry threshold.

Regular-season LPGA wins also are worth one HOF point, meaning if Korda triumphs in either of her final two starts of 2026 — the Annika and the CME Group Championship — she will lock up her place in golf immortality before month’s end.

Players also can earn HOF credits by winning majors (which are worth 2 points); the Vare Trophy for lowest scoring average (1 point); or an Olympic Gold Medal (1 point). Korda’s 69.38 scoring average is tops on tour by a narrow margin but even if she holds on to that edge over the season’s last three events, she still won’t win the Vare because she will not have played the required minimum of 70 rounds.

This isn’t the first time this year that Korda’s Hall of Fame chances have come into focus.

After winning the season’s first two majors — the Chevron and the U.S. Open — Korda’s HOF point tally climbed to 25, leaving her one major title or two non-major victories away from punching her ticket. Not that she was paying much attention. At the season’s third of five majors, the KPMG Women’s PGA, at Hazeltine in late June, Korda confessed to having no clue either how many points are required for Hall of Fame eligibility or how many points she herself had accrued.

“I kind of like to be oblivious about it in that way,” Korda said that week. “I know a lot about the stuff that I want to know about, but this, I don’t want to put extra pressure on myself. I feel like the game of golf is already hard enough. If I add more pressure on myself then it’s going to be even harder. I think it’s an amazing accomplishment and it would be one of the best achievements of my career, for sure.”

Korda is only 28, but that would not make her the youngest player to enter the hall. That honor goes to Lydia Ko, who was 27 years, 3 months, and 17 days when she was inducted in 2024. Ko eclipsed the youthful mark of Inbee Park, who also was 27 when she qualified for the hall in 2016.

title: Takeaways from 2026 Dakar Youth Olympics rugby sevens
article_text:
The 2026 Dakar Youth Olympics rugby sevens has wrapped up, with France and Kenya claiming top honours in Senegal’s capital city.

Marking the third iteration that rugby’s shorter format had taken part in the Youth Olympics, the quality of rugby on display – especially from up-and-coming rugby nations – suggests an exciting new generation of stars could be set to take the game by storm in the coming years.

RugbyPass breaks down the key talking points following the tournament, and where we might expect to see these exciting new athletes next.

Dakar marked the first time the Olympics in any format has ever made it to the African continent – and as evidenced by how the event played out, the city has put forward a compelling case that more events should return.

Complexe Iba Mar Diop proved a perfect setting for rugby action, with 15 different nations clashing in tense contests across three days.

It led to a compelling climax, especially with the likes of local nations like South Africa in the men’s tournament and Kenya and Madagascar in the women’s tournament going deep into finals and being well supported by family and fans.

It further adds to the growing narrative that Africa is an increasingly desirable location to take more rugby events to, with Herbert Mensah, President of Rugby Africa, claiming earlier this year that the region is ready for more global events.

SVNS 2 was also a colossal success in Nairobi early this year – with over 15,000 fans coming through the gate and the tournament set to return to Kenya in a larger venue in January next year – while the Cape Town SVNS has also become an increasingly popular spot on the circuit.

With Dakar’s successful hosting of rugby sevens, such news will likely further impress the powers that be at World Rugby to take more events to growing rugby hotspots in the region.

Of particular note from Dakar was not just the arrival of several new nations who picked up medals, it was the fact that every new nation standing on the podium was from Africa.

Across the three iterations of rugby sevens that have been played at the Youth Olympics, these events have been traditionally dominated by the likes of Australia, France and Argentina – the latter two nations being the only sides to claim medals at all three events.

However, Dakar saw six different nations standing on the podiums of the men’s and women’s events – with the other three being from Africa.

Leading the charge was the Kenya women’s side, the Rising Lionnesses, who after falling to Australia 17-5 in the pool stages bounced back to make the semi finals, then getting revenge defeating the tournament favourites in golden point time, 17-12.

They were well supported by the likes of rising rugby nation Madagascar, who defeated Czechia 26-10 to win bronze in the women’s competition – making history by claiming the first ever medal for their nation at any Olympic event.

The 2026 Youth Olympics also marked the debut of South Africa in the sevens tournament, with the current SVNS Series champions showing they have plenty of depth coming through the ranks, pushing France all the way in the final, but ultimately going down 21-19.

Against some of the strongest rugby programs in the world, the powers that be in Kenya, Madagascar, South Africa, and even the likes of other African nations that didn’t make the podium in Uganda and hosts Senegal have good reason to leave Complexe Iba Mar Diop encouraged.

With all sides looking to push for both SVNS Series and Olympic qualification, the form here suggests their programs are on the right track, with exciting talent in their ranks that have what it takes to compete against the best.

With the Youth Olympics rugby sevens having seen established talent that have gone on to success at Olympic and SVNS Series level, a tournament such as Dakar should give fans early signs for who to watch coming down the pipeline of sevens rugby.

The results should get fans excited that the likes of Kenya and Madagascar can push deep, but also the likes of France, who appear to be building an exciting new generation of men’s players that could challenge the likes of South Africa and New Zealand in the coming years.

Gaspard Laharrague and Matt Lefeuvre headline a strong contingent of players who performed well for the French across the weekend, with their defence particularly strong.

South Africa will also take plenty of confidence from the weekend despite a silver medal finish, with Darnell Delport impressing in several games as his side overcome the likes of 2018 Youth Olympic Games champions Argentina 24-12 in the semi final.

Zain Hido, Josephine Kerubo and Mitchelle Chemtai are also names to remember from the Kenyan women’s side, who grew brilliantly into the tournament and standing up when needed to overcome a more-fancied opponent in Australia in the final.

The Aussies will be bitterly disappointed to miss out on gold, but will at least take confidence that their sevens program is continuing to deliver quality talent, with Darci Mackay and Grace Buchanan headlining a strong squad that performed well until the second half of the final.

The fact the silver medal was the first for the Australian Youth Olympic team at large in Dakar is also something to recognise.

Kenyan captain Zain Hido spoke positively after the final about how much a gold medal like this will do for their program, opening many doors for future investment and opportunities.

title: 2026 Sports Media Update
article_text:
As of May 2026, Arctos is part of KKR Solutions, a new global investing business at KKR spanning investments in premier sports franchises through Arctos Sports and private equity and real assets through Arctos Keystone. Together, these businesses provide bespoke capital solutions, differentiated insights and purpose-built operating capabilities to industry leaders across both markets.

Within Arctos Sports, we focus primarily on investing in professional sports franchises across the four major North American leagues (NFL, NBA, MLB and NHL), supported by deep sector expertise and proprietary research into the factors driving long-term franchise valuations. A key component of our investment thesis is the enduring value of premium live sports media rights, which we believe are becoming increasingly important as streaming reshapes the media landscape and artificial intelligence accelerates content proliferation.

In the analysis below, we examine the evolving sports media rights landscape, the key developments shaping the market in 2026, and why we believe the scarcity and resilience of premium live sports will continue to support long-term growth in franchise valuations.

- The media rights business is transforming in ways that benefit the Big Four (NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL) and other premium sports leagues.

- Competition in the video business has changed forever due to streaming, which now represents over 50% of industry economics. Because the industry is so fragmented, retaining must-have content has never been more important.

- Streaming created an explosion of undifferentiated content, and AI is set to worsen this problem.

- We believe premium live sports is a safe haven that is both AI-resistant and reliably monetizes audiences at scale – an increasingly scarce asset in the content landscape.

Media rights represent an important revenue source for global premium sports leagues, including the “Big Four” in North America (NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL). Media rights deals are typically contracted over multiple years, with annual escalators, and represent a durable driver for franchise valuations. As a firm dedicated to investing in the Big Four and other premium sports, we have spent considerable time and resources on the data and models necessary to understand and forecast media rights values.

We believe three key shifts in the U.S. media marketplace are driving growth in premium sports media rights:

First, the market is digesting the reality of content proliferation, competition and commoditization. Put simply, there is too much video content chasing the same number of eyeballs across the same 24-hour day. Second, a new cohort of streaming-first, diversified tech platforms have emerged as real competitors for sports rights. These businesses are more than just media companies and can amortize rights costs across a broader set of commercial goals. Third, AI is an accelerant: it will make it even easier to create undifferentiated, copiable content at scale, which will worsen the “content glut” and raise the value of anything truly differentiated, authentic and uncopiable.

As a result, traditional media companies face a dilemma. How do media companies protect our subscriber base and advertising business in the face of increasing commoditization and formidable new competitors?

Media companies, both legacy media companies and Big Tech, generate direct revenues from content via subscriptions and advertising – Subscriber Value (SV) and Advertiser Value (AV). Sports media rights packages represent some amount of future SV and AV that leagues and teams sell to media companies in exchange for fixed, contracted revenue – providing certainty and visibility to franchises in exchange for reliable, often exclusive access to must-have content for networks and streamers. That basic set up is in large part not changing, but the number and kind of partners interested in buying rights packages is.

Just over a decade ago, the media business was highly concentrated and consolidated. There was, in fact, only one television product that most households bought: the cable / linear TV bundle. There were only five, scaled, active bidders on sports rights, and even worse for leagues, losing a rights package was less consequential: no one unsubscribed from the bundle because ESPN/ABC lost NASCAR rights in 2014; they just changed the channel. Margins at media networks were ~40%+ - extremely high by any industry standard.

EXHIBIT 1: Video Landscape In the U.S. Is Highly Fragmented

Now, there are at least 11, scaled and capitalized bidders on national and local Big Four sports rights. Most of these players are either streaming-only (Amazon, Netflix, YouTube, Apple) or have both linear and streaming products. Streaming is now >50% of overall industry revenue and ~50% of total media industry EBITDA. The streaming genie is not going back in the bottle: consumer choice is far higher today, and the value proposition is much better. Today, customers can self-curate their own bundle, across many different linear and digital options, and churn at any time. This makes it better than ever to be a media consumer, but harder than ever to be a media company.

As a result, losing must-have sports content today is far more consequential than it was in the bundle world. That would mean risking one of your highest-value subscriber segments to a competitor for as long as the next media deal lasts (often a decade or longer).

There were several important highlights in 2026 worth addressing.

First, viewership and engagement fundamentals in 2026 are stronger than ever. To unpack this, some context-setting is useful. Over the last 10 years, the media business has “unbundled” – this has meant ever increasing fragmentation and narrowing of audiences. Netflix and YouTube have learned your preferences to such precision that they can use machine learning to curate an engagement-maximizing portfolio of content just for you. There is less “mass media” today – in 1980, 52M homes simultaneously watched the evening news on ABC, CBS, or NBC; today that number is 19M, and falling ~2% per year. Movie theater unit ticket sales are half of what they were in 2002. If the market average ratings point for everything in mass culture is facing this headwind, then (as we like to say) “flat is the new up”. And indeed, viewership has been strong in the Big Four and is growing in part due to new measurement standards. Pro sports is one of the last remaining content niches that durably delivers mass, diversified and heterogeneous audiences at scale.

title: Eddie Jones forced to apologise after comments about Wales
article_text:
Eddie Jones was forced to apologise for controversial comments about Wales and Ireland, with the remarks resurfacing ahead of Japan's clash with Wales this weekend.

The Japan head coach will take his side to the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Saturday for their opening autumn Nations Championship fixture.

Both nations will view the encounter as a potential victory, with Wales preparing to face the All Blacks and Australia in their next two matches. Japan, meanwhile, will travel to England and Scotland.

Jones is one of rugby's most experienced coaches, having enjoyed success across several international teams.

He began his coaching career at Randwick before guiding the ACT Brumbies to their first Super Rugby title in 2001.

The Australian subsequently led his country to the 2003 Rugby World Cup final before helping South Africa win the 2007 tournament as an advisor.

Jones later enjoyed a successful spell with Japan, most notably overseeing their famous 2015 Rugby World Cup victory over South Africa.

He then took charge of England, winning consecutive Six Nations titles and reaching the 2019 Rugby World Cup final.

After returning to Australia in 2023, Jones rejoined Japan in 2024.

Back in 2018, Jones "apologised unreservedly" for offensive comments he had made about Wales and Ireland.

The remarks were made during a sponsors' talk in July 2017, when the Australian described Wales as a "s**t little place" and expressed his frustration following a defeat to the "scummy Irish".

Jones, then 58, said he was "very sorry for any offence caused" before adding: "No excuses. I shouldn't have said what I did."

He also revisited Ireland's 13-9 victory over England during the 2017 Six Nations, making it clear that the defeat had continued to frustrate him.

"We've played 23 Tests, we've only lost one Test to the scummy Irish.

"I am still dirty about that game. We'll get that back, we'll get that back don't worry. We've got them next year at home, we'll get them back."

The footage was uploaded to YouTube by Japanese company Fuso in July 2017, but only attracted wider public attention a year later.

During the talk, Jones discussed Japan Under-20s' 125-0 defeat to Wales shortly after his appointment in 2012.

He compared the two countries' populations while discussing their respective rugby histories, using Wales as an example.

"Who knows Wales? Are there any Welsh people here? So it's this little s**t place that has got three million people. Three million!" he said.

Jones has faced further disciplinary action this year after being fined and suspended for six weeks following an incident involving match officials.

In May, the Japan Rugby Football Union barred him from the country's next four matches after he abused officials during an Under-23 tour of Australia.

The governing body additionally imposed a salary reduction on the experienced coach.

Jones accepted the punishment, expressing deep regret and apologising to officials and everyone affected by his inappropriate remarks.

title: Road to the WTA Finals: Early dominance carries Sabalenka to another huge year
article_text:
Editor’s note: Ahead of the year-end tournament, we’re publishing Road to the WTA Finals, an eight-part snapshot of the qualifiers and the form they bring to Indian Wells. Check back all week for new installments.

When you're as dominant as Aryna Sabalenka has been over the past three seasons, you're constantly playing in the shadow of outsized, and in some cases historic, expectations. For Sabalenka, the best player in the world since 2023, an argument could be made that 2026 was a disappointment, without a major and losing the No. 1 ranking after 99 weeks.

Though there's merit to that argument, considering her standard and track record, it's relative. Sabalenka put together another incredible season in 2026, going 47-11 and winning three titles. She was virtually unbeatable in the first quarter of the year, winning 23 of her first 24 matches to start 2026. The apex of her season came during the Sunshine Swing, where she won back-to-back titles in Indian Wells and Miami to become just the fifth player to sweep the Sunshine Double.

She returns to Indian Wells, a welcome destination, for her sixth WTA Finals.

In a nutshell: From early January through the end of March, Sabalenka lost just one match, the Australian Open final to Elena Rybakina. (And she led 3-0 in the third set in that one.) Her level dipped a bit through the spring and summer, reaching just one semifinal in Berlin, but she looked like the Sabalenka of old in New York, dropping just one set in six matches before losing the US Open final to Rybakina.

The match that defined her year: Her incredibly gutsy 3-6, 6-3, 7-6 (6) win over Rybakina in the Indian Wells final, a bona fide match of the year candidate. Just a month and a half after her heartbreaking Australian Open final loss, Sabalenka showed her trademark resilience and fighting spirit in the high-stakes rematch, saving championship point on Rybakina's serve with a cross-court backhand winner. That leveled the third-set tiebreak at 6-all, and Sabalenka won the next two points to claim her first Indian Wells title.

One number to know: 81, Sabalenka's winning percentage in 2026. Though she's tied for fourth in wins, her winning percentage was the highest on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz in 2026.

And we'd be remiss if we didn't mention 99, the number of consecutive weeks that Sabalenka held the No. 1 ranking. It's the sixth-longest streak ever in the top spot.

The social highlight of the year: It's fitting that Sabalenka is returning to Indian Wells, where she not only won the title back in March but also enjoyed some of her most important and memorable off-court milestones. Just before the start of the tournament, Georgios Frangulis proposed to Sabalenka in front of a pool covered in white rose petals, surrounded by an elaborate floral display. The engagement happened the same week that she got her beloved dog, Ash. It was all coming up roses for Sabalenka in early March.

In her words: "My goal has always been to put my name in history, and I just did it. It just sounds so unreal. I don't know how I was able to achieve that, but I'm super proud right now." - Sabalenka, after winning Miami to complete the Sunshine Double

The shot of the year: How about the shot of her life? That's where her mind went after this remarkable point in Madrid.

Attempting to convert her fourth break point of the game against Jaqueline Cristian, Sabalenka showed off her incredible movement and footwork with a running, one-handed backhand passing shot down the line. She had no business getting to that ball, much less hitting a perfect winner, and it even took her by surprise.

What she’s chasing: There's no question that a major-less season, her first since 2022, leaves a sour taste in Sabalenka's mouth. But she can still end her year on a high note with a WTA Finals title, which she's come so close to winning on two occasions. She first made the final in 2022, losing to Caroline Garcia, and then lost to Rybakina in the title match last year. A WTA Finals title is one of the few things missing from her Hall of Fame-caliber resume, and would further boost her status as one of the best players of the last two decades.
